newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pays homage to Jackie Robinson.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pays homage to Jackie Robinson.

text.p: A half century to the day after Jackie Robinson shattered baseball's colour barrier, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday paid tribute to the legendary black athlete and said his legacy was embodied today by golfing superstar Tiger Woods.

Clinton was less than a year old when Robinson took the field with the old Brooklyn Dodgers in a season-opening game against the Boston Braves on April 15, 1947, becoming the first black American to integrate big league baseball in modern times.

Speaking at a political fund-raising luncheon that raised an estimated $700,000 for Democratic candidates in next year's congressional campaign, Clinton hailed the man who went on to a Hall of Fame career as "a highly disciplined, profoundly dignified, greatly talented ballplayer who was prepared not only physically but emotionally and mentally to do what had to be done."

"The same thing happened in the Master's last week," the president said, referring to Woods' record-breaking performance in becoming the first black golfer to win one of golf's most prestigious tournaments. Clinton, an avid golfer, watched the tournament on television.
The White House said he had invited Woods to join him at Shea Stadium to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Robinson's historic accomplishment, but that the 21-year-old phenomenon politely declined.
"He (Woods) felt very strongly that he needed some time out of the limelight, and tonight would very much have been in the limelight, obviously," White House spokesman Barry Toiv said.
Toiv said the president did not feel Woods was snubbing him. Not at all," he said. "Everyone here understood perfectly."

Unlike Woods, who has known mostly adulation, Robinson endured a stream of insults and physical threats from racist fans and players, including some of his own teammates, and went on to such a brilliant career he won over many of his opponents.

Robinson, who died of a heart attack in 1972 at age 53, paved the way for a long line of black players who became major stars over the next 50 years. Clinton was to join Robinson's widow Rachel and dozens of baseball luminaries at an evening ceremony honouring the sports and civil rights hero at Shea Stadium's homeplate.

Fittingly, the ceremony was to take place after the fifth inning of a baseball game between the New York Mets and the Los Angeles Dodgers, the since-transplanted team where Robinson starred on for 10 years before it left Brooklyn.

"I was 10 years old before I ever got a television, and Jackie Robinson had two years in baseball. And I got to watch him on television. I still remember that," Clinton told students at a Brooklyn junior high school anti-smoking rally several hours before the game.

His trip to New York was his first domestic outing since he underwent surgery on March 14 to repair a right knee tendon torn when he stumbled at the Florida home of golf pro Greg Norman. He is still using crutches because of the accident.

In a NBC Radio interview on the eve of the trip, Clinton boasted the United States had made great progress in fighting racial discrimination since Robinson's history-making game, but he said more needed to be done.

"There is no question that it's much better than it was 50 years ago," Clinton said, citing the eradication of legal discrimination and the growth of cross-racial contacts among ordinary people. But he added: "We never finished the job."
"I think that most Americans still don't have ... enough friends, true friends, across racial lines," Clinton said.
